questions.question: What is the difference between a class and an object in Python?
questions.title: Class vs Object in Python
questions.direct_answer: A class defines a new type and its shared behaviour; an object is one concrete instance of that class, with its own identity and usually its own state.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can separate a type definition from the individual values created from it.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling a class only a blueprint without explaining that the class itself is also a runtime object in Python.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use two instances to show shared methods, separate instance state, and distinct identity.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A class creates a new Python type and stores shared attributes and methods.
Calling the class normally creates an instance, also called an object.
Each instance has its own identity and can hold its own attribute values.
Instances find shared methods through their class.
The class is itself an object, so it can be passed around and inspected.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A class is the definition of a Python type. It groups the data names and operations that objects of that type should have. An object is one value created from that class, so it has a separate identity and can store state that differs from other objects.

For example, a `BankAccount` class can define a `deposit` method. `BankAccount("Asha", 500)` and `BankAccount("Ravi", 900)` are two objects: they use the same method definition, but each has a different owner and balance.

When code reads `asha.balance`, Python can find `balance` on that instance. When it reads `asha.deposit`, the method comes from the class and is bound to `asha`. This is how many instances reuse one behaviour definition without sharing all their state.

A class is more than a text template in Python. The class statement runs and creates a class object at runtime, which can be assigned to a variable, passed to a function, or inspected. The practical distinction remains simple: the class describes the type and shared behaviour; an instance represents one actual thing in the program.

sections.title: One definition, many independent instances
sections.content:
A `class` statement executes a block of code and collects its names into a namespace. Python then creates a class object from that namespace. Functions stored there can become methods, while values stored there are class attributes.

Calling the class begins instance creation. The resulting object keeps a reference to its class. In an ordinary class, values assigned through `self`, such as `self.balance`, live on the instance. That is why changing one account's balance does not change another account's balance.

Attribute lookup connects the two levels. Python first considers data controlled by the class, then the instance and class hierarchy according to its lookup rules. A beginner-friendly mental model is that per-object facts belong on the instance, while operations common to every object belong on the class. Shared mutable data needs extra care because a class attribute is one object seen by all instances.

sections.title: Class and object side by side
sections.content:
| Question | Class | Object / instance |
|---|---|---|
| What is it? | A runtime type definition | One value of that type |
| How many? | Usually one class definition | Any number of instances |
| Typical contents | Shared methods and class attributes | Per-instance state |
| Example | `BankAccount` | `BankAccount("Asha", 500)` |
| Identity check | `type(account) is BankAccount` | `account is other_account` compares two identities |

sections.title: Create two objects from one class
sections.content:
```python
class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self.balance += amount

asha = BankAccount("Asha", 500)
ravi = BankAccount("Ravi", 900)
asha.deposit(200)

print(asha.balance)
print(ravi.balance)
print(type(asha) is BankAccount)
print(asha is ravi)
```

The two objects share the `deposit` implementation but keep separate balances and identities.

questions.question: How do attributes and methods work on a Python object?
questions.title: Object Attributes and Bound Methods
questions.direct_answer: Attributes are names reached with dot notation. Instance attributes usually hold per-object state, while a function found on the class becomes a bound method when accessed through an instance.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand dot lookup, per-instance state, class-defined methods, and automatic binding of the instance.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying every attribute is stored inside the object or that Python automatically passes `self` because it is a keyword.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the equivalent class-level function call to make method binding concrete.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Dot notation reads or writes a named attribute.
Assignments such as `self.name = value` normally create instance state.
Methods are functions stored on the class.
Reading a method through an instance binds that instance as the first argument.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An attribute is a named value reached with dot notation, such as `order.total`. It may come from the instance, its class, or a base class. Values assigned as `self.total = amount` normally belong to that individual object.

A method begins as a function stored on the class. When Python evaluates `order.add_item`, the function is returned as a bound method connected to `order`. Calling `order.add_item(25)` therefore has the same basic effect as `Order.add_item(order, 25)`: the instance becomes the first argument.

For example, two `Order` objects can both call the same `add_item` method while updating different `total` attributes. The behaviour is reused from the class, and the state remains on each instance.

Attribute access can be customized with features such as properties and descriptors, so it is not always a plain dictionary lookup. In ordinary interview code, the useful model is instance state plus class behaviour. If lookup cannot find the requested name through the normal path, Python raises `AttributeError`.

sections.title: What the dot connects
sections.content:
The expression before the dot supplies a receiver and the name after it asks Python to resolve an attribute. Ordinary instances often have a `__dict__` containing values assigned directly to them. Their class has another namespace containing functions and shared values, and base classes extend the search.

Functions on a class implement the descriptor protocol. Access through the class, such as `Order.add_item`, gives the underlying function. Access through an instance produces a method object that remembers both that function and that instance. This binding step explains why callers do not explicitly pass the first parameter in `order.add_item(25)`.

Methods can update the receiver because the remembered instance is available inside the function. Other managed attributes, especially `property`, also use the descriptor protocol and may run code during a read or write. Dot syntax is therefore a consistent interface over several kinds of storage and behaviour.

sections.title: How an instance method call is formed
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  E[Evaluate order.add_item] --> L[Find add_item on Order]
  L --> B[Bind function to order]
  B --> C[Call bound method with 25]
  C --> F[Run Order.add_item order, 25]
  F --> S[Update order.total]
```

sections.title: See automatic method binding
sections.content:
```python
class Order:
    def __init__(self):
        self.total = 0

    def add_item(self, price):
        self.total += price

order = Order()
order.add_item(25)
Order.add_item(order, 10)

print(order.total)
print(order.add_item.__self__ is order)
print(order.add_item.__func__ is Order.add_item)
```

Both call forms update the same object. The last two checks expose the instance and function stored by the bound method.
